title: Regional Literature
subtitle: The literary voices of the French-speaking regions

lessons.title: Les voix du Sud
lessons.description: How Southern French writing captures the accent, rhythm, and rural imagination of the Midi — without ever leaving standard grammar behind.

blocks.heading: La musique du Midi
blocks.body: Southern French — the French spoken from Toulouse to Marseille and across Provence — keeps every syllable audible, including the 'e' that falls silent in the north, and stretches its vowels into a sing-song rise and fall. Writers from the region often signal this cadence through word choice, punctuation, and rhythm rather than by respelling words, since standard spelling stays intact even when the sound is unmistakably southern.

examples.french: Chez nous, on dit toutes les syllabes, même les petites.
examples.english: Around here, we say every syllable, even the small ones.
examples.note: a southern speaker explaining the accent

examples.french: Sa voix montait et retombait comme une chanson.
examples.english: His voice rose and fell like a song.
examples.note: describing the accent chantant in prose

examples.french: Il parlait lentement, savourant chaque mot.
examples.english: He spoke slowly, savouring every word.

examples.french: L'accent du Midi ne s'écrit pas, il s'entend.
examples.english: The Midi accent isn't written, it's heard.

examples.french: Ici, même le silence a un accent.
examples.english: Here, even silence has an accent.
examples.note: a common regional turn of phrase

blocks.tip: In C2 reading, treat a marked accent as a narrative signal — it tells you where a character is from before the text says so.

blocks.heading: Une littérature de terroir
blocks.body: Southern regionalist writing grew out of a desire to put rural and small-town Provence, Languedoc, and Gascony on the literary map: markets, vineyards, cicadas, the mistral wind, long summers of farniente. It favours the conteur's voice — warm, digressive, close to oral storytelling — over the terse economy sometimes prized in Paris. None of this makes the register 'less' French; it is simply French with its sleeves rolled up and its feet in the garrigue.

examples.french: Le roman s'ouvrait sur le marché du village, un jour de canicule.
examples.english: The novel opened on the village market, on a scorching day.

examples.french: Elle racontait l'histoire comme on la lui avait racontée, veillée après veillée.
examples.english: She told the story the way it had been told to her, evening after evening.

examples.french: Le narrateur prenait son temps ; ici, personne ne presse un récit.
examples.english: The narrator took his time; here, nobody rushes a story.

examples.french: La couleur locale n'est pas un décor, c'est une manière de voir.
examples.english: Local colour isn't a backdrop, it's a way of seeing.

blocks.tip: This tradition treats digression as a virtue, not a flaw — a straight line to the point can feel cold in a southern tale.

blocks.heading: Mots du pays dans la phrase
blocks.body: Southern writers often drop a single regional word — inherited from Occitan, the old language of the south — into an otherwise perfectly standard French sentence, the way a cook adds one strong spice. The grammar around it stays textbook French; only the word itself carries the accent of the pays.

examples.french: Viens ici, pitchoun, ne reste pas dans le soleil.
examples.english: Come here, little one, don't stay in the sun.

examples.french: Peuchère, la pauvre, elle a dû tout porter seule.
examples.english: Poor thing, she had to carry everything alone.
examples.note: peuchère: a Provençal exclamation of sympathy

examples.french: On sentait déjà l'odeur de la garrigue avant de la voir.
examples.english: You could smell the scrubland before you saw it.

examples.french: Le vieux parlait patois avec ses frères, français avec le maire.
examples.english: The old man spoke patois with his brothers, French with the mayor.

examples.french: Un seul mot d'oc, et toute la phrase sentait le pays.
examples.english: One word of Occitan, and the whole sentence smelled of home.

items.example: On reconnaît son accent du Midi dès la première phrase.
items.exampleEnglish: You recognise his southern accent from the first sentence.

items.example: Le grand-père glissait des mots de patois dans ses histoires.
items.exampleEnglish: The grandfather slipped patois words into his stories.

items.example: Le pitchoun courait pieds nus dans la garrigue.
items.exampleEnglish: The little one ran barefoot through the scrubland.

items.english: regionalism (in literature: a rooted, local voice)
items.example: Le régionalisme méridional a longtemps été mal vu à Paris.
items.exampleEnglish: Southern regionalism was long looked down on in Paris.

items.example: Son écriture garde toute l'oralité des veillées d'autrefois.
items.exampleEnglish: His writing keeps all the orality of old-time storytelling evenings.

items.example: Le chapitre entier tourne autour d'une bouillabaisse partagée.
items.exampleEnglish: The whole chapter revolves around a shared bouillabaisse.

items.example: Le roman s'ouvre sur une partie de pétanque à l'ombre des platanes.
items.exampleEnglish: The novel opens on a game of pétanque in the shade of the plane trees.

items.example: Le dialecte se glisse dans les dialogues, jamais dans la voix du narrateur.
items.exampleEnglish: The dialect creeps into the dialogue, never into the narrator's voice.

items.english: the land's local character (soil, climate, way of life)
items.example: C'est une écriture de terroir, enracinée dans un seul coin de pays.
items.exampleEnglish: It's writing of the terroir, rooted in a single corner of the country.

items.example: Les lecteurs cherchaient une voix authentique, pas une carte postale.
items.exampleEnglish: Readers were looking for an authentic voice, not a postcard.

items.example: La chaleur de l'après-midi ralentit même les phrases.
items.exampleEnglish: The afternoon heat slows down even the sentences.

items.example: Les écrivains du Sud décrivent une lumière presque blanche.
items.exampleEnglish: Southern writers describe an almost white light.

items.example: Le texte flirte avec la nostalgie sans jamais s'y noyer.
items.exampleEnglish: The text flirts with nostalgia without ever drowning in it.

items.example: Le livre entier est une histoire de transmission entre générations.
items.exampleEnglish: The whole book is a story of transmission between generations.

items.example: Ces récits font partie du patrimoine oral de la région.
items.exampleEnglish: These tales are part of the region's oral heritage.

items.example: Le paysage n'est jamais un simple décor dans ces romans.
items.exampleEnglish: The landscape is never just a backdrop in these novels.

items.example: Le récit avance au rythme d'une conversation, pas d'une intrigue.
items.exampleEnglish: The narrative moves at the pace of a conversation, not a plot.

items.example: Son style est savoureux, plein d'expressions du pays.
items.exampleEnglish: His style is richly flavourful, full of local expressions.

items.example: Trois mots suffisent à évoquer tout un été de vacances.
items.exampleEnglish: Three words are enough to evoke a whole summer holiday.

items.example: Tout son œuvre est ancrée dans le Midi.
items.exampleEnglish: His whole body of work is rooted in the South of France.

items.english: Occitan (the historic language of southern France)
items.example: Certains auteurs mêlent français et occitan dans un même dialogue.
items.exampleEnglish: Some authors mix French and Occitan within the same dialogue.

items.example: La langue d'oc a nourri des siècles de poésie méridionale.
items.exampleEnglish: The langue d'oc fed centuries of southern poetry.

items.english: a 19th-century movement to revive southern language and literature
items.example: Le félibrige voulait redonner ses lettres de noblesse à la langue du Sud.
items.exampleEnglish: The félibrige movement wanted to restore the southern language's literary standing.

items.example: Le chant des cigales ouvre presque chaque chapitre.
items.exampleEnglish: The song of the cicadas opens almost every chapter.

items.example: L'odeur de thym et de garrigue traverse tout le texte.
items.exampleEnglish: The smell of thyme and scrubland runs through the whole text.

items.english: the mistral (a strong, cold wind of southern France)
items.example: Le mistral souffle si fort qu'il devient un personnage à part entière.
items.exampleEnglish: The mistral blows so hard that it becomes a character in its own right.

items.english: aïoli (garlic mayonnaise, and the dish built around it)
items.example: Le repas d'aïoli du dimanche rassemble tout le village dans le récit.
items.exampleEnglish: The Sunday aïoli meal brings the whole village together in the story.

items.english: pleasant idleness, doing nothing in particular
items.example: Le roman fait l'éloge du farniente estival.
items.exampleEnglish: The novel sings the praises of summer idleness.

items.example: On lui a reproché de forcer la couleur locale.
items.exampleEnglish: He was criticised for overdoing the local colour.

items.example: Le narrateur se pose en simple conteur de village.
items.exampleEnglish: The narrator presents himself as a simple village storyteller.

items.example: Le style doit tout à la tradition orale des veillées.
items.exampleEnglish: The style owes everything to the oral tradition of storytelling evenings.

items.example: Elle a gardé son accent chantant même après vingt ans à Paris.
items.exampleEnglish: She kept her lilting accent even after twenty years in Paris.

items.english: pastis (aniseed apéritif, and its social ritual)
items.example: Les dialogues les plus vrais se passent autour d'un pastis.
items.exampleEnglish: The most truthful dialogue happens over a pastis.

items.english: gift of the gab, easy talkativeness
items.example: Le vieux pêcheur avait une faconde qui tenait toute la place en haleine.
items.exampleEnglish: The old fisherman had a gift of the gab that kept the whole square hanging on his words.

items.example: Son tempérament méridional perce dans chaque page.
items.exampleEnglish: His southern temperament shows through on every page.

items.example: Chaque chapitre s'ouvre sur un vieux dicton du pays.
items.exampleEnglish: Every chapter opens with an old local saying.

blocks.heading: Représenter l'accent sans casser la langue
blocks.body: Southern writers rarely respell words to fake an accent — that would tip into caricature. Instead they signal the accent through rhythm markers: short exclamations, repeated interjections, and sentences that trail with an extra beat. The grammar underneath stays entirely standard; only the texture around it changes.

examples.french: Allez, viens, on va être en retard, té !
examples.english: Come on, let's go, we'll be late, come on!
examples.note: "té" is a rhythmic filler, not a grammar change

examples.french: Il a dit ça tout doucement, en traînant sur les voyelles.
examples.english: He said it very softly, drawing out the vowels.

examples.french: — Alors, qu'es aco ? demanda-t-il, mi-français mi-occitan.
examples.english: "So, what's that?" he asked, half in French, half in Occitan.

examples.french: La phrase s'étirait, comme si elle avait tout son temps.
examples.english: The sentence stretched out, as if it had all the time in the world.

blocks.tip: At C2 level, learn to hear the accent in punctuation and rhythm, not in misspelled words — that distinction separates respectful regionalism from mockery.

blocks.heading: Le régionalisme lexical dans une syntaxe standard
blocks.body: A single occitanism or Provençal borrowing can sit inside a completely standard French clause without disturbing its grammar: word order, agreement, and tense stay textbook. What changes is register — the sentence suddenly feels local, warm, specific. Recognising this lets you read regional prose without mistaking regional vocabulary for grammatical error.

examples.french: Le pitchoun s'est endormi sous le figuier.
examples.english: The little one fell asleep under the fig tree.
examples.note: standard passé composé, one regional noun

examples.french: Elle a préparé l'aïoli comme sa grand-mère le lui avait appris.
examples.english: She made the aïoli the way her grandmother had taught her.

examples.french: On y allait, peuchère, sans se plaindre.
examples.english: We went along, poor souls, without complaining.

examples.french: Le patois revenait dans sa bouche dès qu'il était en colère.
examples.english: The patois came back to his lips as soon as he got angry.

items.prompt: Listen. What does the speaker mean?
items.french: Il a un accent chantant, on sent tout de suite qu'il vient du Midi.
options: He has a singsong accent, you can tell right away he's from the South.
He can't sing at all, everyone knows it.
He refuses to speak French properly.
He just moved to Paris last month.
items.answer: He has a singsong accent, you can tell right away he's from the South.

items.prompt: Listen. What literary quality is being described?
items.french: Ce roman appartient à une littérature de terroir, ancrée dans le paysage et l'oralité.
options: A regionalist novel, rooted in landscape and oral storytelling.
A science-fiction novel set in space.
A courtroom drama with no setting described.
A grammar textbook for beginners.
items.answer: A regionalist novel, rooted in landscape and oral storytelling.

items.prompt: Listen and type what you hear.
items.french: Le mistral soufflait si fort que les volets claquaient.
items.answer: Le mistral soufflait si fort que les volets claquaient.
acceptedAnswers: le mistral soufflait si fort que les volets claquaient

items.prompt: Listen carefully and write the full sentence, including the regional word.
items.french: Peuchère, la pauvre bête a marché tout l'après-midi sous la chaleur.
items.answer: Peuchère, la pauvre bête a marché tout l'après-midi sous la chaleur.
acceptedAnswers: peuchere la pauvre bete a marche tout lapres-midi sous la chaleur

items.prompt: Read this southern-flavoured sentence aloud, letting every syllable land.
items.french: On a le temps, ici ; rien ne sert de courir sous ce soleil.
items.english: We've got time here; there's no point rushing under this sun.
items.tip: Stretch the vowels slightly and don't drop the final 'e' sounds — that's the whole southern rhythm.

items.prompt: Say this line the way a village conteur might deliver it.
items.french: Et voilà, pitchoun, c'est comme ça que ton grand-père a rencontré ta grand-mère.
items.english: And there you go, little one, that's how your grandfather met your grandmother.
items.tip: Slow down before 'pitchoun' — a storyteller pauses to draw the listener in.

items.prompt: Practise this exclamation of sympathy in context.
items.french: Peuchère, elle a dû tout porter seule jusqu'au village.
items.english: Poor thing, she had to carry everything alone all the way to the village.
items.tip: "Peuchère" carries warmth, not pity from above — say it gently, almost like a sigh.

passages.title: Le marché du jeudi
passages.french:
Le jeudi, le village entier descendait vers la place, dès l'aube, avant que la chaleur n'écrase les pavés.
Sur les étals, les melons voisinaient avec les tomates, et l'odeur du thym montait de la garrigue toute proche.
— Approchez, approchez, criait le marchand, mes tomates ont mûri sous le vrai soleil, pas sous une lampe !
Sa voix chantait plus qu'elle ne parlait, montant sur la dernière syllabe comme une question qu'il ne posait pas.
Une vieille femme s'arrêtait devant chaque étal, soupesait un fruit, le reposait, en repartait sans un mot.
— Peuchère, disait-elle enfin, tout a tellement changé depuis que je suis pitchoune.
Les cigales, déjà, s'étaient mises à chanter dans les platanes, comme si elles aussi avaient un marché à tenir.
Au bout de la place, deux hommes jouaient à la pétanque à l'ombre, sans se presser, sans compter les heures.
Le mistral s'était levé pendant la nuit et avait nettoyé le ciel d'un bleu presque douloureux.
On entendait, entre deux phrases de français, un mot de patois glissé comme une signature.
Le boulanger, lui, gardait sa fournée du matin pour ceux qui viendraient après midi, par fidélité plus que par calcul.
Une odeur d'aïoli flottait déjà depuis la maison du maire, où l'on préparait le repas du dimanche en avance.
Les enfants couraient entre les jambes des adultes, pieds nus, indifférents à la chaleur qui écrasait les autres.
Le vieux conteur du village, assis sur son banc habituel, attendait qu'on vienne lui demander une histoire.
Il ne la racontait jamais deux fois de la même façon, et personne, ici, ne le lui reprochait.
Quand midi sonna au clocher, la place se vida d'un coup, comme si le soleil avait donné le seul ordre qui comptât.
passages.english:
On Thursdays, the whole village came down to the square at dawn, before the heat crushed the cobblestones.
On the stalls, melons sat next to tomatoes, and the smell of thyme rose from the nearby scrubland.
"Come closer, come closer," shouted the vendor, "my tomatoes ripened under real sun, not under a lamp!"
His voice sang more than it spoke, rising on the last syllable like a question he wasn't asking.
An old woman stopped at every stall, weighed a piece of fruit in her hand, put it back, and moved on without a word.
"Poor thing," she finally said, "everything has changed so much since I was a little girl."
The cicadas had already started singing in the plane trees, as if they too had a market to keep.
At the far end of the square, two men played pétanque in the shade, unhurried, uncounting the hours.
The mistral had risen overnight and swept the sky into an almost painful blue.
Between two French sentences, you could hear a word of patois slipped in like a signature.
The baker kept his morning batch for those who would come after noon, out of loyalty more than calculation.
A smell of aïoli already drifted from the mayor's house, where Sunday's meal was being prepared early.
Children ran between the adults' legs, barefoot, indifferent to the heat that crushed everyone else.
The village's old storyteller, sitting on his usual bench, waited for someone to ask him for a tale.
He never told it the same way twice, and here, nobody held that against him.
When noon struck at the bell tower, the square emptied at once, as if the sun had given the only order that mattered.

lessons.title: Les lettres belges et suisses
lessons.description: Belgian and Swiss French have their own literary identity — a taste for the surreal, a habit of precision, and a vocabulary all their own.

blocks.heading: Une francophonie sans complexe
blocks.body: Belgium and French-speaking Switzerland are not satellites of Paris — they are old, independent centres of French-language writing, each with its own institutions, prizes, and publishing houses. Their literature has never needed to sound French from France; it sounds Belgian, or it sounds Swiss, and that is simply what French looks like when it grows in more than one soil.

examples.french: La Belgique et la Suisse romande ont leurs propres académies et leurs propres prix littéraires.
examples.english: Belgium and French-speaking Switzerland have their own academies and their own literary prizes.

examples.french: On n'écrit pas 'en attendant Paris', on écrit chez soi.
examples.english: You don't write 'waiting for Paris', you write at home.
examples.note: a common rebuttal to the idea that Belgian or Swiss French is provincial

examples.french: Le plurilinguisme du pays infuse toute son écriture.
examples.english: The country's multilingualism runs through all its writing.

examples.french: Aucune de ces deux traditions ne s'excuse d'exister.
examples.english: Neither of these two traditions apologises for existing.

blocks.tip: Treat 'belgicisme' and 'helvétisme' the way you'd treat any regional variety of English — a different norm, not a mistake.

blocks.heading: Le goût belge de l'insolite
blocks.body: A recurring thread in Belgian French writing is a taste for the surreal and the slightly uncanny: ordinary streets, ordinary objects, tipped just a few degrees off balance until the everyday starts to feel strange. This isn't confined to one movement or one century — it resurfaces across genres, from prose to graphic storytelling, as a kind of national reflex.

examples.french: La rue semblait tout à fait normale, sauf que personne n'y projetait d'ombre.
examples.english: The street seemed perfectly normal, except that nobody cast a shadow on it.

examples.french: L'insolite s'installe sans bruit, entre deux phrases banales.
examples.english: The uncanny settles in quietly, between two ordinary sentences.

examples.french: Le récit garde un ton posé même quand tout devient absurde.
examples.english: The narrative keeps a level tone even as everything turns absurd.

examples.french: C'est un surréalisme discret, presque poli.
examples.english: It's a discreet, almost polite kind of surrealism.

blocks.heading: La précision suisse, entre les langues
blocks.body: Swiss French writing often carries a reputation for precision and restraint — a legacy, some say, of a country that governs itself in four languages and cannot afford ambiguity. Its literature is also marked by the linguistic frontier itself: the 'Röstigraben', the informal divide between French-speaking and German-speaking Switzerland, shows up again and again as a subject and a source of dry humour.

examples.french: Chaque mot est pesé comme s'il coûtait cher.
examples.english: Every word is weighed as if it cost something.

examples.french: De l'autre côté du Röstigraben, on ne raconte pas les histoires de la même façon.
examples.english: On the other side of the Röstigraben, stories aren't told the same way.

examples.french: La Suisse romande écrit dans l'ombre attentive de ses trois autres langues nationales.
examples.english: French-speaking Switzerland writes in the attentive shadow of its three other national languages.

examples.french: Rien n'est exagéré ; tout est mesuré, jusqu'à l'understatement.
examples.english: Nothing is exaggerated; everything is measured, right down to the understatement.

blocks.tip: Don't mistake Swiss restraint for coldness — the emotion is there, just carefully rationed.

items.example: Le texte est truffé de belgicismes assumés.
items.exampleEnglish: The text is peppered with unapologetic belgicisms.

items.example: Certains helvétismes surprennent un lecteur parisien.
items.exampleEnglish: Some helvetisms surprise a reader from Paris.

items.example: Le personnage a septante ans et ne s'en cache pas.
items.exampleEnglish: The character is seventy and doesn't hide it.

items.example: Elle a vécu huitante ans dans le même village.
items.exampleEnglish: She lived eighty years in the same village.

items.example: Le récit s'étend sur nonante années d'histoire familiale.
items.exampleEnglish: The story spans ninety years of family history.

items.example: Le roman s'ouvre sous une drache bien bruxelloise.
items.exampleEnglish: The novel opens under a proper Brussels downpour.

items.example: Toute l'action se déroule dans un kot d'étudiant à Louvain.
items.exampleEnglish: The whole plot takes place in a student's digs in Louvain.

items.example: Le narrateur a facile pour raconter le malheur des autres.
items.exampleEnglish: The narrator finds it easy to tell other people's misfortunes.

items.example: Toute la famille se retrouve autour du souper.
items.exampleEnglish: The whole family gathers around the evening meal.

items.example: Le personnage principal écrit ses meilleures pages au déjeuner.
items.exampleEnglish: The main character writes his best pages at breakfast.

items.example: Son natel sonne au pire moment du dénouement.
items.exampleEnglish: Her mobile phone rings at the worst moment of the ending.

items.example: La grand-mère range sa panosse avant de raconter son histoire.
items.exampleEnglish: The grandmother puts away her floor cloth before telling her story.

items.example: — Merci pour l'accueil. — Service !
items.exampleEnglish: "Thanks for having me." "You're welcome!"

items.example: — On se retrouve à midi ? — Ça joue.
items.exampleEnglish: "Shall we meet at noon?" "That works."

items.example: Le surréalisme belge préfère les rues tranquilles aux rêves criards.
items.exampleEnglish: Belgian surrealism prefers quiet streets to loud dreams.

items.example: On loue souvent la précision de la prose suisse romande.
items.exampleEnglish: The precision of French-Swiss prose is often praised.

items.example: Écrire depuis la marge de la francophonie a ses avantages.
items.exampleEnglish: Writing from the margin of the French-speaking world has its advantages.

items.example: La francophonie ne se résume pas à la France.
items.exampleEnglish: The French-speaking world is not just France.

blocks.heading: Les nombres en septante, huitante, nonante
blocks.body: Belgian and Swiss French replace the famously awkward French counting system (soixante-dix, quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix) with straightforward decimal forms: septante (70), huitante or octante (80, mostly in Switzerland), and nonante (90). Grammatically they behave exactly like any other number — same agreement, same position — so a literary text can switch a single number and instantly place its setting outside France.

examples.french: Elle a septante-trois ans et refuse de le dire à voix haute.
examples.english: She's seventy-three and refuses to say it out loud.

examples.french: Le vieux café a fêté ses nonante ans le mois dernier.
examples.english: The old café celebrated its ninetieth anniversary last month.

examples.french: En France on dirait quatre-vingt-dix ; ici, on dit nonante, un point c'est tout.
examples.english: In France they'd say quatre-vingt-dix; here, we say nonante, full stop.

examples.french: Huitante n'existe presque qu'en Suisse, et encore, pas partout.
examples.english: Huitante exists almost only in Switzerland, and even then, not everywhere.

blocks.tip: Never mark septante or nonante as an 'error' in a Belgian or Swiss text — they are simply the local standard, as correct as soixante-dix is in France.

blocks.heading: Des tournures venues d'ailleurs, une syntaxe intacte
blocks.body: Constructions like 'avoir facile' (to find something easy) or the exclamation 'service !' (you're welcome) look unusual to a reader used to Hexagonal French, but they follow their own stable, internal logic rather than breaking any rule. Recognising them as regional norms — not slips — is part of reading Belgian and Swiss prose at a C2 level.

passages.title: Le train de Genève
passages.french:
Le train partait de Bruxelles à sept heures précises, et déjà cela m'étonnait : rien, chez nous, ne part jamais tout à fait à l'heure.
Ma tante habitait Genève depuis nonante ans, ou presque, et parlait de la Suisse comme d'un pays qu'elle avait dû apprendre par cœur.
— Ici, disait-elle au téléphone, on ne dit pas soixante-dix, on dit septante, et personne ne discute.
Le paysage changeait lentement : d'abord la drache belge, puis, plus loin, un ciel plus net, presque rincé.
J'avais grandi entre deux langues et trois frontières linguistiques, sans jamais trouver cela extraordinaire.
Mon grand-père, lui, disait toujours qu'un vrai Bruxellois se moque de tout, même de son propre accent.
À la frontière, un douanier suisse vérifia mon passeport avec une précision presque comique, comme s'il pesait chaque mot.
— Vous venez pour le travail ou pour la famille ? demanda-t-il, sans lever vraiment les yeux.
— Pour le souper de ma tante, répondis-je, et il sourit, comme si cette réponse suffisait à tout expliquer.
Genève apparut enfin, rangée, presque trop calme après le désordre chaleureux de Bruxelles.
Ma tante m'attendait sur le quai avec un cornet de marrons chauds, comme chaque année.
— Alors, dit-elle, toujours de l'autre côté du Röstigraben, à vivre entre deux mondes ?
Je répondis que je n'avais jamais vu cela comme deux mondes, plutôt comme une seule maison à deux étages.
Elle rit, de ce rire suisse qui ne fait presque pas de bruit, et me prit le bras.
Le soir, au souper, elle me raconta encore comment on l'avait appelée nonante fois « l'étrangère de Bruxelles » avant qu'on l'appelle simplement par son prénom.
Je l'écoutai comme on écoute une histoire qu'on connaît déjà, et qu'on veut pourtant réentendre.
passages.english:
The train left Brussels at exactly seven o'clock, and that alone surprised me: back home, nothing ever leaves quite on time.
My aunt had lived in Geneva for nearly ninety years, and spoke of Switzerland like a country she'd had to learn by heart.
"Here," she'd say on the phone, "we don't say soixante-dix, we say septante, and nobody argues."
The landscape changed slowly: first the Belgian downpour, then, further on, a clearer sky, almost rinsed clean.
I had grown up between two languages and three language borders, without ever finding that extraordinary.
My grandfather always said a true Brussels native makes fun of everything, even his own accent.
At the border, a Swiss customs officer checked my passport with an almost comic precision, as if weighing every word.
"Are you here for work or for family?" he asked, without really looking up.
"For my aunt's supper," I answered, and he smiled, as if that answer explained everything.
Geneva finally appeared, tidy, almost too calm after Brussels' warm disorder.
My aunt was waiting on the platform with a paper cone of hot chestnuts, like every year.
"So," she said, "still on the other side of the Röstigraben, living between two worlds?"
I answered that I had never seen it as two worlds, more like a single house with two floors.
She laughed, that quiet Swiss laugh that makes almost no sound, and took my arm.
That evening, at supper, she told me again how she'd been called "the stranger from Brussels" ninety times over before people simply called her by her name.
I listened the way you listen to a story you already know, and still want to hear again.

lessons.title: La littérature québécoise
lessons.description: Québécois writing and its most distinctive register, joual — the spoken French of working-class Montreal turned into literary voice.

blocks.heading: Une langue à part entière
blocks.body: Québécois French developed for four centuries with limited contact with France, absorbing English loanwords, keeping older French forms alive, and shifting the meaning of everyday words. The result is not 'accented French' — it is a fully-formed regional French, with its own literature, its own prizes, and its own readers who never think of themselves as speaking an imperfect version of anything.

examples.french: Le français québécois n'est pas une déformation, c'est une évolution parallèle.
examples.english: Québécois French isn't a distortion, it's a parallel evolution.

examples.french: On y trouve des mots que la France a oubliés depuis trois siècles.
examples.english: You find words there that France forgot three centuries ago.

examples.french: Une littérature entière s'est construite dans cette langue, sans complexe.
examples.english: An entire literature was built in this language, without any inferiority complex.

examples.french: Le lecteur français doit parfois s'adapter, et non l'inverse.
examples.english: Sometimes it's the French reader who has to adapt, not the other way around.

blocks.tip: Never call Québécois French 'bad French' — that framing is exactly what this unit exists to dismantle.

blocks.heading: Le joual, une langue de la rue devenue littérature
blocks.body: Joual is the informal, urban register of Québécois French historically associated with working-class Montreal — marked by contracted pronouns, dropped negation, and English borrowings. Starting in the 1960s, writers began putting joual directly on the page and on stage, not as comic relief but as a legitimate literary voice capable of carrying serious drama, exactly as regional and working-class registers do in any literature.

examples.french: Chu tanné, moi, de toujours dire pardon pour comment je parle.
examples.english: I'm sick of always apologising for how I talk.
examples.note: chu = je suis; tanné = fed up

examples.french: T'as-tu fini, oui ou non ?
examples.english: Are you done, yes or no?
examples.note: "-tu" here is a spoken question marker, not the pronoun "you"

examples.french: On n'a pas d'argent, pis on n'en aura pas demain non plus.
examples.english: We don't have money, and we won't have any tomorrow either.

examples.french: Le joual sur scène a choqué avant d'émouvoir.
examples.english: Joual on stage shocked before it moved audiences.

blocks.heading: Une voix, pas un accident
blocks.body: When a Québécois narrator writes in joual, it is a deliberate choice of register, the same way a novelist elsewhere might choose formal, literary French for effect. The narration can shift between standard French description and joual dialogue within the same page — a contrast that carries meaning, marking class, intimacy, or defiance, never carelessness.

examples.french: Le narrateur décrit la scène en français soutenu, puis laisse parler ses personnages en joual.
examples.english: The narrator describes the scene in formal French, then lets his characters speak in joual.

examples.french: Ce passage d'un registre à l'autre est un choix, pas une erreur.
examples.english: That shift from one register to another is a choice, not a mistake.

examples.french: Le joual porte la colère du personnage mieux qu'aucun mot soutenu ne le pourrait.
examples.english: Joual carries the character's anger better than any formal word could.

examples.french: Écrire en joual, c'était refuser de s'excuser d'être d'ici.
examples.english: Writing in joual was a refusal to apologise for being from here.

blocks.tip: Read joual dialogue aloud slowly at first — the contractions (chu, y, pis, ben) become intuitive once you hear the rhythm.

blocks.heading: Les traits grammaticaux du joual
blocks.body: Joual has consistent, rule-governed features rather than random 'errors': the contraction of 'je suis' to 'chu', dropped 'ne' in negation, 'y' for 'il' or 'ils', and 'pis' for 'puis'. A C2 reader should recognise these as a coherent phonological and grammatical system — one that can be written down deliberately for literary effect, the same way any dialect is transcribed in world literature.

examples.french: Chu pas capable de faire ça tout seul.
examples.english: I'm not able to do that alone.
examples.note: chu = je suis; ne dropped before 'pas'

examples.french: Y savait pas trop quoi dire.
examples.english: He didn't really know what to say.

examples.french: On a mangé, pis on est parti.
examples.english: We ate, and then we left.

examples.french: J'la connais depuis qu'on est tout-petits.
examples.english: I've known her since we were little.

blocks.tip: When transcribing joual, contractions follow the sound of fast, natural speech — read the line aloud and the spelling usually explains itself.

blocks.heading: La particule interrogative -tu
blocks.body: In spoken Québécois French, adding '-tu' after the verb turns a statement into a yes/no question, a construction with deep roots in older French but rarely used this way in France today. It has nothing to do with the pronoun 'tu' — it functions purely as a question marker and can attach to any subject, singular or plural.

examples.english: Is it true, what they're saying?

passages.title: Le dépanneur du coin
passages.french:
Le dépanneur ouvrait à six heures, été comme hiver, et mon oncle y était toujours le premier client.
— Ben, disait-il en poussant la porte, encore frette à matin, hein ?
Le commis, derrière la caisse, ne levait même pas les yeux pour répondre.
— Ouais, pis on dirait que ça va pas s'arranger avant la fin de semaine.
Mon oncle prenait toujours la même chose : un café, un journal, et une conversation qu'il n'avait pas vraiment envie d'avoir.
Il avait grandi dans cette ruelle, entre le dépanneur et l'école, et il ne s'était jamais vraiment demandé s'il fallait en avoir honte.
— Chu tanné de l'hiver, disait-il chaque matin de janvier, comme une prière qu'il savait inutile.
Le commis souriait, pis répondait toujours la même affaire.
— C'est-tu déjà arrivé, un hiver qui finit pas ? On verra ben.
Ma tante racontait que mon oncle avait appris à lire dans ce dépanneur, un journal à la fois, un mot à la fois.
Elle disait ça avec une fierté qu'elle ne cachait pas, même si personne ne le lui avait demandé.
Le samedi, toute la gang se retrouvait sur le perron d'à côté pour jaser jusqu'à ce que le soleil tombe.
On parlait de rien, pis c'était exactement pour ça qu'on aimait ça.
Mon oncle disait que le vrai luxe, dans la vie, c'était d'avoir une place où personne te demande de parler autrement.
Asteure, le dépanneur a fermé, mais le perron, lui, est encore là.
Pis chaque fois que je passe devant, j'entends encore sa voix, ben distincte, qui demande si l'hiver va finir un jour.
passages.english:
The corner shop opened at six, summer and winter alike, and my uncle was always its first customer.
"Well," he'd say, pushing the door open, "cold again this morning, eh?"
The clerk, behind the till, wouldn't even look up to answer.
"Yeah, and it looks like it's not going to get better before the weekend."
My uncle always ordered the same thing: a coffee, a newspaper, and a conversation he didn't really want to have.
He had grown up in that alley, between the corner shop and the school, and had never really asked himself whether he should be ashamed of it.
"I'm so sick of winter," he'd say every January morning, like a prayer he knew was useless.
The clerk would smile, and give the same answer every time.
"Has a winter ever actually ended? We'll see, I guess."
My aunt used to say my uncle had learned to read in that shop, one newspaper at a time, one word at a time.
She said it with a pride she didn't hide, even though nobody had asked her to explain.
On Saturdays, the whole crew would gather on the porch next door to chat until the sun went down.
We talked about nothing, and that was exactly why we loved it.
My uncle used to say that the real luxury in life was having a place where nobody asked you to talk differently.
Now the corner shop has closed, but the porch is still there.
And every time I walk past, I can still hear his voice, perfectly distinct, asking whether winter will ever end.

questions.prompt: What does the uncle's daily routine at the corner shop suggest about the text?
options: It shows how ordinary, repeated moments carry deep meaning and identity.
It shows the uncle dislikes reading newspapers.
It shows the shop is about to close permanently that same day.
It shows the family has just moved to Montreal.
questions.answer: It shows how ordinary, repeated moments carry deep meaning and identity.

options: A place where nobody asks him to speak differently.
Having enough money to travel abroad.
Never having to talk to anyone.

questions.answer: A place where nobody asks him to speak differently.

items.prompt: What is joual?
options: The informal, urban register of Québécois French, historically tied to working-class Montreal.
A formal register used only in academic writing.
A dialect spoken exclusively in rural France.
A synonym for verlan.
items.answer: The informal, urban register of Québécois French, historically tied to working-class Montreal.
